structure.title: Chapters 1–4 · Gateshead · Who gets to tell what happened?
structure.text: John Reed finds Jane reading behind a curtain and decides she has no business with the family books. By the time the adults arrive, the child who struck back is the one in trouble. Jane tells the incident years later, with enough of her original fury intact for the reader to feel what it cost her to be called wicked.

structure.title: Chapters 5–10 · Lowood · A school can give a girl two educations
structure.text: At school, a public accusation can follow Jane as effectively as it did at home. This time there are also people willing to hear her account. While she learns the subjects that will let her earn a living, she studies Helen Burns and Miss Temple for answers to a harder question about how to live with an injustice.

structure.title: Chapters 11–27 · Thornfield · Her employer wants her company
structure.text: Jane goes to a country house to teach a little girl. Its owner begins asking for her opinion and seems to enjoy it most when she answers him plainly. The evenings grow precious to Jane. The man whose good opinion matters to her also owns the house where she sleeps and pays her wages.

structure.title: Chapters 28–38 · Beyond Thornfield · A decision has a price in pounds and meals
structure.text: The later part of the novel takes Jane's convictions out into a world of roads, work, shelter and dependence on strangers. A person who refuses a life someone else has arranged still needs a place to eat that evening. Brontë takes the time to account for both sides of that decision.

people.name: Jane Eyre
people.role: An orphan who tells her own history
people.text: Jane remembers what it was like to be ten years old and to have been given a terrible account of one's own character by nearly everyone in the room. Her older voice can recognise how little she then understood without surrendering the child's conviction that she had been wronged.

people.name: Edward Rochester
people.text: Rochester asks questions whose bluntness would startle most guests in a drawing room. His enjoyment of Jane's replies is one of the first sustained pleasures of her adult life. He also knows much of the household's history that its young governess cannot learn by asking him a question in return.

people.name: Helen Burns and Miss Temple
people.role: Jane's friend and teacher at Lowood
people.text: Helen has an account of forgiveness that Jane finds both moving and hard to accept. Miss Temple offers food, warmth and a hearing. Brontë lets the child who fought back at Gateshead learn from both women without making her anger disappear overnight.

context.title: A governess lives at work
context.text: Knowing enough to teach a gentleman's child qualifies Jane to take part in conversations around her. A wage and a room are what make it possible for her to stay. In a household like Thornfield, the person who takes an interest in her ideas can also determine whether she has a home.

context.title: The same religious vocabulary in different mouths
context.text: One adult invokes God to justify putting a child to shame. Another understands a duty before God as a reason to hear that child fairly. Christianity runs through the book in voices sufficiently different for Jane to have to decide what each speaker is asking her to accept.

notice.text: Follow the book John takes from Jane.
notice.why: Before it becomes a weapon, it has been Jane's shelter on a wet afternoon. When John declares that the books belong to his family, a dispute about a possession becomes a dispute about who has any right to pleasure in that house.

passages.quote: There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.

notice.text: Notice when Rochester gives Jane a chance to contradict him.
notice.why: A frank answer delights him. It can cost her considerably more to give it. A conversation may feel wonderfully equal for an evening while both speakers retain very different powers over what will happen the next morning.

notice.text: Hear the older Jane turn to the reader.
notice.why: She can invite the reader into her confidence or make us wait a little before she tells us what happened. The girl who had such trouble getting a fair hearing at Gateshead has grown into the woman who decides just when the rest of us may hear her story.

opening: As a child, Jane Eyre thinks she would endure almost anything to be loved. She grows up poor and becomes a governess, accustomed to being useful rather than wanted, until her employer begins seeking her company and enjoying the frankness others have punished. She falls in love with him. When keeping that love would require her to betray her convictions, Jane must face the possibility of being alone again, with very little to live on and every reason to want to stay.
